Exercise A

Reading: My Year in Osaka

Read the text carefully, then answer the questions below.

Before you read — optional, not marked
This is just to get you thinking — you can leave it empty and it does not count towards your score.
My Year in Osaka

When I arrived in Osaka for my exchange year, I was sure I had prepared for everything. I had studied Japanese for three years, packed the right clothes and read every guidebook I could find. If I had known how different daily life would feel, I might have worried less about vocabulary lists and more about the small things — how to queue, when to bow, and why nobody ever says “no” directly.

The first month was the hardest. If you misread a social signal in Japan, people rarely correct you — they simply go quiet. I remember asking my host mother if I could help with dinner, and her gentle “It’s fine” actually meant “Please sit down”. Had I understood that earlier, I would have saved myself a lot of embarrassment.

Things changed when I stopped translating every sentence in my head and started watching people instead. I learned that politeness is not about perfect grammar but about attention. If I felt lost, I asked — but softly: “Would you mind showing me how this works?” instead of “What does this mean?”

By the time I flew home, the quiet shops and careful routines that had confused me felt almost normal. Culture shock never disappears completely, but if you give it time, it turns into something valuable: the habit of looking twice before you judge.

Comprehension & the if-clause at work

1 How had the narrator prepared for her exchange year?

2 What did the host mother’s “It’s fine” actually mean?

3 What changed things for the narrator after the first month?

4 How did the narrator ask for help once things had changed?

5 In “Had I understood that earlier, I would have saved myself a lot of embarrassment”, what structure is “Had I understood”?

6 (Review from an earlier unit) In “I remember asking my host mother if I could help”, what job does “asking” do?

Exercise B

If-Clauses: Real, Unreal & Past Conditions

Choose the correct form to complete each sentence about life abroad.

Reminder Real condition: If you give it time, it will turn into something valuable. Unreal now: If I were you, I would watch first and judge later. Unreal past: If I had known, I would have worried less.
If-clauses

1 If you ___ to a country with a different culture, you will notice things you never questioned at home.

2 If I had known about the gift customs, I ___ such an expensive present.

3 If she ___ more attention to how people greet each other, she would learn the rules faster.

4 You will settle in much faster if you ___ the local language a little every day.

5 If they had warned me about the silent family dinners, I ___ so nervous at my first meal.

6 If you ___ homesick, call a friend from home — then go out and do something local.

7 We ___ the festival completely if our host brother hadn’t explained it to us.

8 If I could give just one piece of advice, it ___ this: watch first, judge later.

Exercise C

Polite Requests

Choose the word or phrase that makes each request polite and correct.

Reminder Would you mind + -ing (or if + past): Would you mind showing me the way? Could you + verb · I was wondering if you could … · Would you be so kind as to …
Polite requests

1 ___ you mind if I sat here? All the other seats are taken.

2 Excuse me, could you ___ me where the nearest pharmacy is?

3 I was wondering if you ___ help me fill in this form.

4 Would you mind ___ a photo of us in front of the temple?

5 ___ it be all right if I came a little later tomorrow?

6 Do you think you ___ speak a little more slowly, please?

7 Could I ask you ___ the window? It’s very warm in here.

8 Would you be so kind ___ to write the address down for me?

Exercise D

Writing: A Welcome Email

A new exchange student from Osaka is joining your class next month, and your teacher has asked you to send her a short welcome email.

Your task

Write a short email (60–100 words) to Hana, the new exchange student. Welcome her and give her advice about dealing with culture shock in the first weeks. Use at least two if-clauses and at least one polite request phrase (for example: Would you mind…?, Could you…?).
